prediction:
1) Congenital cutaneous meningiothelial hamartoma / primary cutaneous meningioma
   - Rationale: Present since birth on the scalp with overlying alopecia and absent follicular ostia; firm, subcutaneous lesion with sharp margins and no intracranial/bone invasion on MRI; punch biopsy shows monomorphic ovoid cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm forming whorls and strands around collagen — classic meningothelial (whorled) morphology.
   - Key confirmatory tests: immunohistochemistry (EMA and progesterone receptor positivity, vimentin positive, cytokeratin negative).

2) Proliferating trichilemmal (pilar) tumor / trichilemmal cyst (proliferating variant)
   - Rationale: Common on the scalp, congenital/longstanding pilar cysts can enlarge after trauma and can be firm and subcutaneous with overlying alopecia; may be lobulated and firm on biopsy although typical keratinization features would be expected.
   - Key confirmatory tests: cytokeratin profile, demonstration of trichilemmal keratinization on deeper specimen.

3) Cutaneous adnexal tumor (e.g., cylindroma/spiradenoma)
   - Rationale: Scalp is a predilection site; cylindromas show nodular, sometimes whorled architecture and can present as firm congenital lesions that cause alopecia.
   - Key confirmatory tests: histologic features on excision, IHC (cytokeratins, EMA) and look for characteristic jigsaw/palisading architecture.

4) Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP)
   - Rationale: Firm subcutaneous lesion that can be adherent to deeper tissues; may infiltrate dermis and subcutis and produce loss of follicular ostia/alopecia; less likely given whorled histology and congenital onset but important to consider because of local aggressiveness.
   - Key confirmatory tests: CD34 immunostain (usually diffusely positive) and excision specimen to assess infiltrative margins.

5) Dermoid/epidermoid cyst with secondary changes (less likely)
   - Rationale: Congenital scalp masses are often dermoids; clinical MRI and punch biopsy findings argue against a simple dermoid (epidermis spared, no adnexal structures on biopsy), but a deeper dermoid/dermoid variant could present similarly and enlarge after trauma.
   - Key confirmatory tests: excision and full histopathologic review to look for adnexal structures and cyst lining.

Recommended next steps (high priority)
- Perform immunohistochemistry on the biopsy specimen: EMA, progesterone receptor, vimentin, cytokeratins, S-100, CD34. (Most critical: EMA/PR positivity would support meningothelial origin.)
- Obtain a contrast-enhanced MRI (if not already performed with contrast) or CT of the calvarium to definitively evaluate any osseous defect or communication with intracranial compartment.
- Refer to dermatologic surgery/plastic surgery (and neurosurgery if any suggestion of bone defect/communication) for complete excisional biopsy with clear margins for definitive diagnosis and treatment.
